prime.problem: An eval is only as honest as the thing that marks each run. If the marker reads the agent's final message, or asks a model that saw what the agent saw, a run that ended with a failing test can still be scored as a pass.
prime.fits: You met tasks, trials and hidden tests in Measuring an agent, and the claim chain in 'Done' is a chain of states. This card opens up the grader: what it reads, which kind to use, and in what order.
expect: code grader vs model judge vs human
prime.goal: Given an agent and a task, pick graders for it, say what each one reads, put them in the right order, and explain why a judge that sees only the agent's view adds little.

attend: Why does Wolfe insist the outcome is the state of the environment, not the agent's text, and which Tuesday-run grader depends on that?
What does the transcript grader catch that the outcome grader doesn't need, and what would it miss if the agent re-ran pytest on edited tests?
Why does the judge pass the Tuesday run on the compacted view but not on the full trace?
When do two grading layers stop multiplying their miss rates together?
Which of the seven steps exists to check the grader itself rather than the agent?

must: The agent's text and the world can disagree → grade the outcome (environment state) rather than the output → a fresh pytest re-run fails the Tuesday run even though step 9 says every test passes

Code graders are fast, reproducible and need a reference; judges handle subjective criteria but are noisy and biased → run deterministic checks first and stop on a hard fail → a judge never gets to average a broken outcome into a good score

A judge can only object to what is in the text it reads → if it reads what the agent saw (the compaction summary), it inherits the agent's blind spot → its misses line up with the agent's mistakes, so it adds little as a layer

Layers that miss independently multiply: 0.30 × 0.40 × 0.20 = 2.4% slip through (illustrative) → if one layer's holes sit where another's are, that layer adds nothing (6.0%) → choose layers that read different evidence
elevated: Judges must be calibrated against human labels and the agreement kept under watch → a judge or rubric change is a change in the ruler → test grader changes against a frozen human-labelled set, or a score move may be the grader, not the agent
reference: the three judge setups: pairwise, pointwise (for example 1–5), reference-guided
Wolfe's suggestion of 10 to 20 starter tasks
τ-bench's ###STOP### end marker and the 54.04 / 41.64 string checks
the names of the seven steps in order
the weighted-composite score with a threshold

compress.prompt: Card closed: in 3–5 sentences, define the five words using the Tuesday run, then say which three graders you'd run on it, in what order, and what each would say. Or draw the Swiss-cheese picture with one pair of aligned holes and label why they line up.
checklist: task, trial, transcript and outcome, with the outcome as world state, not the agent's text
code on the outcome: re-run pytest outside the agent → FAIL
code on the transcript: claim vs the last test result → FAIL, a false success claim
a judge only for subjective parts, and blind if it reads only the agent's view
deterministic first; a judge never overrides a hard fail
independent layers multiply miss rates; aligned holes don't

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between an output and an outcome, and why Wolfe's restaurant example makes it matter for graders.
answer: output: the text the agent produces
outcome: the final state of the environment after the trial
an agent can write "The restaurant is booked!" with no booking, so a grader on the output passes a failed trial

retrieve.q: Walk through the layered gate on the Tuesday run: which grader runs first, what it reads, what it returns, and whether the judge is ever asked.
answer: outcome grader re-runs pytest on the final files → exit 1 → FAIL
the gate stops at the first hard fail: "FAIL at outcome; judge not consulted"
the transcript grader would also fail it: step 9 claims success, step 6 was exit 1 with no later run

retrieve.q: You have a budget for one extra grading layer. Do you add a second LLM judge from the same model family as the agent, or a sampled human review? Justify with how layers combine.
answer: layers help by multiplying miss rates only if their misses are independent
a same-family judge reading similar text is likely to miss the same failures (aligned holes)
a human reads differently and also calibrates the judge, so it is the better extra layer despite cost

retrieve.q: Why does Wolfe's step 4 ask for a reference solution for every task, even though the agent never sees it?
answer: it proves the task is solvable
it checks that the grader passes a known-good answer, so failures are agent failures, not grader or task bugs
like Terminal-Bench's oracle solutions

compare.q: Measuring an agent asked how many trials and how wide the interval is; this card asks what marks each trial. What is fundamentally different about the two problems, and how does each fail?
answer: that card treats each trial's pass/fail as given and fights randomness with repeats and intervals
this card asks whether that pass/fail is true at all
the stats fail by being too narrow; the grader fails by being biased, so more trials of a wrong grader give a confident wrong number

compare.q: The claim chain splits "done" into five links. Which link does each of the three Tuesday graders check, and why do the two code graders sit on different links?
answer: outcome grader: link 4, effect verified, from outside the agent
transcript grader: compares link 3 (command succeeded, exit 1) with the delivered claim, so it names the false success claim
the judge on the agent's view reads only the delivered claim and the summary, so it checks no link independently

compare.q: Compaction rewrote "exit 1" as "tests passing". Why does that same lossy step decide what a judge can see, and what is the fix on the grading side?
answer: the judge given the agent's working set reads the inflated summary, not the step-6 result
so the status inflation passes straight into the grade
fix: grade from the full trace and the outcome, never from the working set

predict.q: Change the Tuesday run: after compaction the agent edits the test file so test_parse_due_date asserts nothing, re-runs pytest (exit 0) and then claims success. Which of the three graders now pass it, and what would you add?
predict.answer: The transcript grader passes it: the last test run in the transcript is now exit 0, so the claim matches. A judge on either view likely passes it too. The outcome grader passes as well if it runs the repo's own, edited tests. Only a grader that uses tests the agent could not touch (hidden or restored originals) or a process check on "no test files changed" catches it. That is why the outcome grader must own its reference.
